purpose: Agalsidase beta is used to treat a rare inherited condition called Fabry disease. In Fabry disease, your body does not make enough of an important enzyme called alpha-galactosidase A. This medication replaces that missing enzyme to help prevent the harmful buildup of fatty substances in your body.
how_it_works: Your body normally uses an enzyme called alpha-galactosidase A to break down a fatty substance called GL-3. In Fabry disease, this enzyme is missing or not working well, causing GL-3 to build up and damage organs like the kidneys, heart, and nervous system. Agalsidase beta is a lab-made version of this enzyme that is given through an IV infusion to do the job your body cannot do on its own.
common_side_effects: Infusion reactions are the most common side effects and can include fever, chills, flushing, headache, nausea, tiredness, and a fast heartbeat during or after the IV infusion. These reactions often get better over time as your body adjusts to the medication. Your care team will monitor you closely during each infusion.
warnings: Some patients can have serious allergic or infusion reactions, including severe ones like anaphylaxis, so you will always be watched carefully during treatment. Tell your doctor right away if you develop hives, difficulty breathing, chest tightness, or feel faint. Your doctor may give you pre-medications like antihistamines or steroids before each infusion to help reduce the risk of reactions.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is 1 mg per kilogram of body weight, given as an IV infusion every 2 weeks. Infusions are typically given in a clinic or infusion center and can take about 2 to 4 hours depending on how well you tolerate the medication. Your doctor will adjust the infusion rate based on how your body responds.
